items.plain: Don't hold back or force out your tears because other people are watching; tears are most shameful when they are faked. Let them come naturally.
items.core_idea: Let tears flow naturally, never feigned for an audience

items.plain: You can follow nature in grief and still keep your dignity. Grief can have a grace of its own; the wise keep a measure even in tears, while the unwise let sorrow and joy overflow.
items.core_idea: Grief can be genuine and still dignified

items.plain: Accept calmly what cannot be avoided. Nothing that happens is truly unheard of or new; right now countless people are arranging funerals and mourning, while you have already finished your mourning.
items.core_idea: Death is common; accept the inevitable calmly

items.plain: You may talk often about the one who died and treasure his memory. That memory will come back more often if you greet it without bitterness, since no one wants to keep company with sorrow.
items.core_idea: Welcome memories of the dead without bitterness

items.plain: Mourning wildly and then forgetting the dead is how animals love their young, fiercely and then not at all. A sensible person should keep remembering the dead but stop mourning them.
items.core_idea: Keep remembering the dead, but stop mourning

items.plain: To someone grieving an early death, say this: compared with eternity, young and old alike live almost no time at all, yet we foolishly treat our tiny lives as if they were vast.
items.core_idea: Against eternity, every life is equally brief

items.plain: Every day and hour shows how small and fragile we are, reminding us of the weakness we forget; while we plan as if we will live forever, they make us glance back at death.
items.core_idea: Daily life reminds us of our fragility and death

items.plain: It is foolish to map out your whole life when you don't even own tomorrow. Planning to get rich and then retire assumes too much; everything is uncertain, and chance cuts into even the hour you are living.
items.core_idea: Don't count on the future; tomorrow isn't yours

items.plain: Fate has set a limit to each life, but no one knows how close theirs is. So live as if you had reached the end: put nothing off, and settle life's accounts every day.
items.core_idea: Live each day as if it were your last

items.plain: Life's great flaw is that part of it is always put off. Someone who completes their life each day never lacks time; postponing breeds fear and craving for the future, and worry about what's coming is the most miserable thing.
items.core_idea: Postponing life breeds anxiety about the future

items.plain: Begin living right now, and treat each day as a whole life. Whoever lives that way is at ease, while those who live only on hope find the future slipping away, replaced by greed and fear of death.
items.core_idea: Treat each day as a complete life

items.plain: We must drop our craving for more life; suffering will come at some point anyway. What matters is not how long you live but how nobly, and living nobly often means not living long.
items.core_idea: How nobly you live matters, not how long

items.plain: The human soul is great and noble; it accepts no limits except those it shares with the gods.
items.core_idea: The soul is great and accepts no small limits

items.plain: As the womb readies us for life outside it, life readies us for another birth. So await your last hour without fear, the body's end but not the soul's; treat your things like luggage, since you must move on.
items.core_idea: Life prepares the soul for another birth

items.plain: The day you dread as the end of everything is really the day your eternal life begins.
items.core_idea: Death is the birthday of eternity

items.plain: Why look for disasters that may never come, like fires or collapsing buildings? Accidents are rare; the danger you face every day comes from other people. Guard against that, because no harm is more common or more sly.
items.core_idea: Everyday danger comes from people, not accidents

items.plain: In dealing with others, do no harm so that you are not harmed. Share in everyone's joys and sympathize with their troubles, while remembering what to give and what to hold back.
items.core_idea: Harm no one; share others' joys and troubles

items.plain: Coming back to life for others' sake shows a great heart. The highest kindness is to guard your health in old age more carefully because someone you love wants you to.
items.core_idea: Caring for yourself for a loved one's sake

items.plain: Told that a man's travels did him no good, Socrates said he had taken himself along. To escape your troubles you need a new self, not a new place; wherever you go, you bring your own character.
items.core_idea: You can't escape your troubles by travelling

items.plain: If you count wealth as a good, you will feel poor whenever a neighbor is richer. If you prize status, others' promotions will torment you, and your ambition will make you feel last if anyone is ahead.
items.core_idea: Valuing wealth and status breeds endless envy

items.plain: Once your mind has learned blind panic, you won't feel safe even when you are, and it can't protect itself. It flees danger instead of avoiding it, and we are most exposed when we turn our backs.
items.core_idea: Panic makes us more vulnerable, not safer

items.plain: New friends won't be the same, but neither will you; you change every hour, though you notice it less in yourself. Swinging between hope and despair breeds trouble; if you are wise, mix the two.
items.core_idea: Everyone changes; balance hope with despair

items.plain: Rushing from place to place won't help, because you carry your emotions and troubles with you, and they press on you from every side. A sick person needs medicine, not a change of scenery.
items.core_idea: Troubles need a cure, not a change of scenery

items.plain: The only safe harbor from life's storms is to stop fearing the future, stand firm, and be ready to take whatever fortune throws at you head-on, without hiding or turning away.
items.core_idea: Stand firm and face fortune head-on

items.plain: Many things that seem terrifying at night look laughable in daylight.
items.core_idea: Night fears look ridiculous by day

items.plain: We don't lack confidence because things are hard; things are hard because we lack confidence.
items.core_idea: Difficulty comes from lack of confidence

items.plain: Give up the gold, silver and possessions that weigh down a wealthy home; freedom has a price. If you value freedom highly, you must value everything else little.
items.core_idea: Freedom requires valuing possessions little

items.plain: Whoever is feared is also afraid; no one has spread terror and still lived with peace of mind.
items.core_idea: Those who are feared live in fear

items.plain: Nothing helps more than staying quiet, talking little with others and much with yourself. Conversation coaxes secrets out of us, and no one keeps what they hear to themselves, so a secret soon becomes common talk.
items.core_idea: Talk little; secrets never stay secret

items.plain: The surest path to peace of mind is never to do wrong. Wrongdoers live in fear and restlessness; their conscience gives them no ease, and even if they escape notice, they never feel sure they have.
items.core_idea: A clear conscience is the basis of peace

items.plain: No one is truly at the mercy of their affairs. People tangle themselves up in them by choice, then tell themselves that being busy proves they are happy.
items.core_idea: Busyness is chosen, and it isn't happiness

items.plain: We overdo everything, even reading and study, so we end up learning to perform in the classroom rather than to live.
items.core_idea: Learn for life, not for show

items.plain: Life is like a public bath, a crowd or a journey: things get thrown at you or hit you by accident. On this rough road you will slip, fall, tire, lose companions and bury people, and must keep going.
items.core_idea: Life is a rough journey; keep going

items.plain: People face dangers bravely when they have prepared for them long in advance, while the unprepared panic over trifles. So make sure nothing catches you off guard; constant reflection lets you meet any trouble like an adult, not a novice.
items.core_idea: Prepare in advance so nothing catches you off guard

items.plain: Winter brings cold, summer heat, bad weather illness, and floods or fires bring losses. We cannot change this order of things, but we can build brave hearts that endure chance and live in harmony with nature.
items.core_idea: We can't change nature, only our courage

items.plain: Whatever happens, assume it had to happen, and don't rail against nature. Endure what you cannot change and follow without complaint the God who guides all things; only a bad soldier grumbles at his commander.
items.core_idea: Endure what you cannot change without complaint

items.plain: A prayer to the Master of the heavens: lead me wherever you wish and I will follow quickly. Even if unwilling, I will go and suffer anyway; fate leads the willing soul and drags the unwilling.
items.core_idea: Fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling

items.plain: Don't grab at knowledge randomly or all at once; you know the whole by studying its parts. Take on only what you can handle and absorb what you can hold; a sound mind grows as it takes in more.
items.core_idea: Learn in parts, at a pace you can handle

items.plain: It is easy to stir someone to want goodness, because nature has planted the seeds of virtue in all of us. When something prompts it, the good spirit wakes as if freed from chains.
items.core_idea: The seeds of virtue are in everyone

items.plain: The poor lack many things; the greedy lack everything. A greedy person helps no one and harms himself most.
items.core_idea: Greed impoverishes and harms the greedy most

items.plain: Someone who wants little needs little.
items.core_idea: Want little and you need little

items.plain: The best days of our unhappy human life go by first; then come sickness, bitter old age and toil, until harsh death takes everything away.
items.core_idea: Life's best days pass first

items.plain: Just as the best wine pours from the top of the jar and the dregs sink to the bottom, the best part of life comes first. Should we let others drink the best and keep the dregs for ourselves?
items.core_idea: Life's best part comes first; don't waste it

items.plain: So let us work with courage and single purpose, skipping distractions, so we don't realise too late how fast time flies. Welcome each day as it comes as the best one, and make it truly yours.
items.core_idea: Welcome each day as the best and use it

items.plain: People prove their words are truly their own by doing what they talk about.
items.core_idea: Your words are yours when you act on them

items.plain: Good people help each other, because each gives the other's virtues exercise and keeps wisdom sharp. Everyone needs someone to compare notes and think things through with.
items.core_idea: Good people sharpen each other's virtues

items.plain: It is natural to love our friends and rejoice in their success as our own; without this, even virtue fades. Virtue asks us to plan and think carefully, and that is easier with a friend.
items.core_idea: Friendship strengthens virtue and clear thinking

items.plain: People see others' affairs more clearly than their own, because self-love blinds them and fear in danger clouds their judgment. Wisdom begins when a person is calm and free of fear.
items.core_idea: Wisdom begins when fear and self-love fall away

items.plain: Look at how things really are, not how people describe them, and you'll see that misfortunes help us more than they harm us. Hardship has often started happiness, while welcomed privileges have often led people to a cliff edge.
items.core_idea: Misfortune often helps more than it harms

items.plain: If you are wise, measure everything by the human condition and limit both your joys and your fears. Don't rejoice in anything for long, so you won't fear anything for long.
items.core_idea: Limit joy so you limit fear

items.plain: There is no reason to think anything is truly fearful; the things that unsettle us are empty. We pass fear to each other without ever examining what we dread, so falsehood survives because no one challenges it.
items.core_idea: Our fears are empty because we never examine them

items.plain: Just as children cower in fear in the dark, grown adults feel afraid even in broad daylight.
items.core_idea: Adults fear in daylight as children fear the dark

items.plain: What you truly need is found everywhere; what you don't need always has to be hunted down with great effort.
items.core_idea: Necessities are easy; luxuries take effort

items.plain: Turn to true riches: learn to be content with little, and boldly say that with water and porridge you could rival Jupiter in happiness. Better still, need not even those, since happiness shouldn't depend on gold or on porridge.
items.core_idea: Happiness should depend on nothing external

items.plain: If you think on these things often, you will try not to look happy but to be happy, and to seem happy to yourself rather than to others.
items.core_idea: Be happy, not merely seem happy

items.plain: People love and hate their own vices at the same time.
items.core_idea: We love and hate our vices at once

items.plain: Bravery is an unbreakable fortress for our human weakness. Someone protected by it can endure life's siege without anxiety, because they rely on their own strength and their own weapons.
items.core_idea: Bravery is a fortress for human weakness

items.plain: Posidonius said you are never safe relying on weapons fortune gave you; fight with your own. Fortune never arms you against herself, so those armed against enemies are defenseless against fortune.
items.core_idea: Rely on inner strength, not fortune's gifts

items.plain: Alexander conquered nation after nation, yet he lay in the dark lamenting a friend he killed or lost, beaten by anger and grief. He aimed to control everything except his own emotions.
items.core_idea: Conquering the world isn't conquering yourself

items.plain: People are badly mistaken who think they prosper by conquering ever more territory. They know nothing of the kingdom as great as the heavens: command over yourself is the greatest command of all.
items.core_idea: Self-command is the greatest command

items.plain: Everyone should first be convinced that they must be just without reward, and should even take pleasure in freely upholding justice. Don't look for a reward for doing right; the just act itself pays more.
items.core_idea: A just act is its own reward

items.plain: Those who want their virtue noticed are after fame, not virtue. You must be willing to be just without praise, often even while disgraced; if you are wise, take delight in a bad name earned by doing right.
items.core_idea: Be just without needing recognition

items.plain: We'd want less if we saw how little we can consume and for how short a time. Nothing helps moderation more than remembering that life is short and uncertain; whatever you do, keep death in mind.
items.core_idea: Remembering death teaches moderation

items.plain: Money costs us tears and toil. Greed is miserable both in craving and in getting; owning wealth brings more anguish than gaining it, losses hurt more than they should, and whatever we fail to add feels like loss.
items.core_idea: Wealth brings more misery than it relieves

items.plain: If those who crave wealth or office could talk with people who have them, they'd change their prayers: the successful always chase more and scorn what they've got. No one is content; everyone prefers what they missed.
items.core_idea: No one is satisfied by what they win

items.plain: Every vice has its excuse and starts small and easy to manage, then spreads; once begun, you can't be sure it will stop. Every emotion starts weak and grows, so it's easier to prevent than to give up.
items.core_idea: Stop vices and passions before they start

items.plain: Love stirs us whether returned or rejected, and easy love troubles us as much as hard love. Knowing our weakness, let us stay calm and keep our unsteady spirit away from drink, beauty, flattery and other temptations.
items.core_idea: Know your weakness and avoid temptation

items.plain: As far as we can, let us step back from slippery places; even on dry ground it is hard enough to stand firm.
items.core_idea: Avoid temptation; standing firm is hard enough

items.plain: Nature has given us enough strength, if only we use it and gather our powers to help us rather than hinder us. The real reason is unwillingness; the excuse is inability.
items.core_idea: We are unwilling, not unable

items.plain: Life has handed you so many unsolved problems, and you are still splitting hairs? Stop practising with toy weapons; you need real armour. Teach me how to keep sadness and fear from my soul and shed hidden cravings. Do something!
items.core_idea: Stop theorising and deal with real troubles

items.plain: Nature hasn't given us so much time that we can waste any. Illness, family troubles, business and sleep already take much of it. With so short and swift a life, why spend most of it on useless things?
items.core_idea: Life is too short to waste on trivia

items.plain: How much happier is the person who watches the scramble for office, power, wealth and family without caring, asking nothing of anyone and telling Fortune, I want no favours from you. That cuts Fortune down to size.
items.core_idea: Asking nothing of Fortune makes you free

items.plain: What we chase looks grand only because we are far below it; to those who reach it, it is just a rung on the ladder. Misled by the crowd, people win their wish and find it bad, empty or disappointing.
items.core_idea: What we chase looks great only from afar

items.plain: Would you rather have much, or enough? Whoever has much wants more, proof they don't have enough yet; whoever has enough has what the rich never get: a place to stop.
items.core_idea: Enough gives what wealth never does: a stopping-point

items.plain: Money has never made anyone rich; it only makes people crave more of it, because having more lets them reach for still more.
items.core_idea: Money only breeds a craving for more

items.plain: The Builder of the universe, who set the laws of life, meant us to live well but not in luxury. All we need for well-being lies close at hand; luxury can only be gathered with misery and anxiety.
items.core_idea: Needs are easy; luxury brings misery

items.plain: Nothing satisfies us, though we are already dying, nearer the edge every hour. It is a mistake to fear only the last day, since every day counts toward death; the last hour arrives, but every hour approaches it.
items.core_idea: We are dying every day, not just the last

items.plain: Being one consistent person is a great role, but only the wise manage it; the rest of us keep changing masks, thrifty one day, wasteful the next. Keep the character you began with, so people at least recognise you.
items.core_idea: Be one consistent person throughout life

items.plain: Infancy, boyhood, youth and old age are different stages, but I, who have lived through each, am still the same person.
items.core_idea: Through every stage of life, I remain myself

items.plain: We work harder and are better people when we rise early and greet the dawn; it is shameful to lie dozing when the sun is high, or wake only at noon, which still feels like dawn to many.
items.core_idea: Rising early makes us better and more diligent

items.plain: Arriving tired at my villa late at night to find nothing ready, I use the delay to reflect: nothing is heavy if you accept it lightly, and nothing need anger you unless you add to your troubles by getting angry.
items.core_idea: Accept things lightly and they weigh little

items.plain: Get used to plain food, since circumstances catch out even the rich. No one can have whatever they wish, but anyone can stop wishing for what they lack and cheerfully use what comes. An uncomplaining stomach brings independence.
items.core_idea: Freedom lies in not wanting what you lack

items.plain: We don't notice how much is unnecessary until it's gone; we used things because we had them and bought them because others did. We follow convention instead of reason, as if being common made something right.
items.core_idea: Live by reason, not by what others do

items.plain: Like a catchy tune after a concert, flatterers' praise of wrong things sticks in our minds and keeps returning. So shut your ears to bad talk from the start, before the words settle in and grow bolder.
items.core_idea: Shut out bad talk before it takes root

items.plain: No one is good by accident; virtue must be learned. Pleasure is petty and shared with animals, and glory is empty. Poverty harms only those who fight it, and death is no evil but something all people share equally.
items.core_idea: Virtue must be learned; death is shared by all

items.plain: Why work so hard on strength, beauty, hair or speed, when cattle are stronger, lions have finer manes and hares are faster? Stop competing where you must lose and return to the good that really is yours.
items.core_idea: Seek the good that is truly your own

items.plain: Count yourself happy only when your joys come from reason and nothing people grasp or pray for makes you desire it. You come into your own when you see that the world's fortunate are the most unfortunate of all.
items.core_idea: The world's fortunate are truly the least fortunate

items.plain: We too have a religion, given to our ancestors and handed down to us. It teaches us to be thankful, to stay united and to love one another, and we never quarrel about religion.
items.core_idea: Our religion teaches thanks, unity and love

items.plain: My ancestors worshipped the Great Mystery in silence and alone, without seeking anything for themselves. Silent, because words are always weak; alone, because God is nearer in solitude, and no priest stood between a person and the Maker.
items.core_idea: Worship of the Great Mystery is silent and solitary

items.plain: People who live outdoors know that solitude builds a kind of inner force that crowds quickly drain. Even their enemies admit the American Indian has an unmatched inner power and composure, independent of circumstances.
items.core_idea: Solitude builds inner strength that crowds drain

items.plain: Even if you admire natural law, science hasn't explained everything. The origin of life is the supreme mystery at the heart of worship, and before it we, like the naturalist, can only see the Divine in creation with awe.
items.core_idea: Life's origin remains a mystery that calls for awe

items.plain: Among our people, old age was in some ways the happiest time of life. It brought freedom from hard and dangerous work and from the rules of custom and manners everyone else had to follow.
items.core_idea: Old age brings freedom and happiness

items.plain: For the Indian, the one unavoidable duty was prayer, the daily recognition of the Unseen and Eternal, needed more than food. At dawn he bathes and faces the rising sun in silent prayer; each soul meets the Great Silence alone.
items.core_idea: Daily silent prayer at dawn, alone

items.plain: Whenever a hunter comes upon a beautiful or awe-inspiring sight, like a rainbow over a mountain or a red prairie sunset, he pauses to worship. He needs no weekly holy day, because to him every day is God's.
items.core_idea: Every day is holy; worship where beauty appears

items.plain: Friendship is the hardest test of character. Loyalty to family is easy, and love between man and woman is mixed with desire and self-interest. To have a friend and stay true through every trial is the mark of a man.
items.core_idea: True friendship is the hardest test of character

items.plain: Long before I heard of Christ or met a white man, an unschooled woman, with Nature's help, taught me the heart of morality. I knew God, understood goodness and loved true beauty; civilization has taught me nothing better.
items.core_idea: Nature taught me goodness; civilization added nothing better

items.plain: As a child I knew how to give, but I lost that grace once civilized. Then any pretty pebble was precious and every tree sacred; now I worship with the white man before a painted landscape priced in dollars.
items.core_idea: Civilization traded natural reverence for price tags

items.plain: The first Americans joined pride with humility and saw speech as a dangerous gift, not proof of superiority. They held silence to be perfect balance of body, mind and spirit; the ideal was a self unshaken by life's storms.
items.core_idea: Silence is perfect balance of body, mind, spirit

items.plain: The old chief Wabashaw said: hold your tongue when young, and in old age you may develop a thought that will help your people.
items.core_idea: Silence in youth ripens wisdom for age

items.plain: We believed love of possessions is a weakness to overcome, because it upsets the spirit's balance. So children learned generosity early, giving away what they valued most and handing out the family's gifts, and heard stories shaming the stingy.
items.core_idea: Love of possessions upsets the spirit; teach generosity

items.plain: The true Indian puts no price on his property or work; only his strength limits his generosity. He counts a hard or dangerous task an honour and would be ashamed to ask a reward, leaving thanks to the one served.
items.core_idea: Give generously and ask no reward

items.plain: A truly brave person gives in to neither fear nor anger, desire nor pain, and is always master of themselves; such courage rises to chivalry, patriotism and real heroism.
items.core_idea: True bravery is mastery of yourself

items.plain: An old chief told a scout setting out in midwinter to hunt for a starving people: let no cold, hunger, pain, danger, nor even death, or the fear of them, stop you from doing a good deed.
items.core_idea: Let nothing stop you from doing good

items.plain: The Indian's attitude to death, the test and backdrop of life, fits his whole outlook: it holds no terror for him. He meets it simply and calmly, seeking only an honourable end as a last gift to his family.
items.core_idea: Meet death calmly, with honour

items.plain: The Indian never doubted the soul is immortal but didn't speculate about the afterlife. He believed the spirit the Great Mystery breathed into us returns to Him, pervades nature, and may linger near the grave, hearing prayers.
items.core_idea: The spirit returns to the Great Mystery and pervades nature

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that nothing prevents ill will or removes it like the heart's release through love. When you focus your mind wisely on loving-kindness, ill will doesn't arise, or if it has, it fades.
items.core_idea: Loving-kindness prevents and dissolves ill will

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that nothing prevents restlessness and remorse or removes them like a settled mind. When the mind is settled, they don't arise, or if they have, they go.
items.core_idea: A settled mind dissolves restlessness and remorse

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that nothing brings as much happiness as a developed and cultivated mind. A trained mind brings happiness.
items.core_idea: A trained mind brings happiness

items.plain: Just as you can't see the bottom of a muddy lake, a mendicant whose mind is clouded can't know what is good for themselves or others, or reach the noble ones' higher knowledge, because their mind is clouded.
items.core_idea: A clouded mind cannot see what is good

items.plain: The Buddha says he sees nothing that changes as quickly as the mind, so quickly that it's hard even to find a comparison for it.
items.core_idea: Nothing changes faster than the mind

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that the mind is radiant by nature, but it gets stained by defilements that come and visit it.
items.core_idea: The mind is radiant but stained by visiting defilements

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that nothing grows good qualities and weakens bad ones like contentment. When you are content, the skillful grows and the unskillful fades.
items.core_idea: Contentment grows good qualities

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that nothing grows good qualities and weakens bad ones like having good friends. With good friends, the skillful grows and the unskillful fades.
items.core_idea: Good friends grow good qualities

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that losing wealth is a small thing; losing wisdom is the worst loss.
items.core_idea: Losing wisdom is worse than losing wealth

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that losing fame is a small thing; losing wisdom is the worst loss.
items.core_idea: Losing wisdom is worse than losing fame

items.plain: The Buddha says that when someone has right view, all their deeds, intentions and choices lead to good, pleasant results, just as a good seed of sugarcane or grape makes everything it absorbs taste sweet.
items.core_idea: Right view makes every action bear good fruit

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that developing one thing calms body and mind, settles thinking, and fully develops every quality needed for realization: mindfulness of the body.
items.core_idea: Mindfulness of the body calms and awakens

items.plain: The Buddha says two things cause remorse: having done bad things and having failed to do good things, in body, speech and mind. Thinking of either, a person feels mortified.
items.core_idea: Bad done and good undone both cause remorse

items.plain: The Buddha says he learned two things: never be satisfied with good qualities, and never stop trying. Even if only skin and bones remained, he kept striving to reach what human effort can achieve; it was by diligence he awakened.
items.core_idea: Awakening comes through unrelenting effort

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants to give up what is unskillful. It is possible, or he wouldn't say so; and since doing it leads to welfare and happiness rather than harm, he urges it.
items.core_idea: Giving up the unskillful is possible and brings happiness

items.plain: Two kinds of people are wise: one who recognizes their own mistake, and one who properly accepts another person's confession of a mistake.
items.core_idea: Wise people admit mistakes and accept apologies

items.plain: Two things lead to realization: serenity and discernment. Serenity develops the mind, which lets go of greed; discernment develops wisdom, which lets go of ignorance. A mind stained by greed isn't free, and wisdom clouded by ignorance can't grow.
items.core_idea: Serenity frees from greed; discernment frees from ignorance

items.plain: The Buddha says you could never repay your parents, even by carrying them for a hundred years or making them rulers of the earth, for they raised you. But helping them grow in faith, ethics, generosity or wisdom repays them.
items.core_idea: Parents can be repaid only by helping them grow spiritually
items.extended_text: Mendicants, I say that these two individuals cannot easily be repaid. What two? Mother and father. You would not have done enough to repay your mother and father even if you were to carry your mother around on one shoulder and your father on the other, and if you lived like this for a hundred years, and if you were to anoint, massage, bathe, and rub them; and even if they were to defecate and urinate right there. Even if you were to establish your mother and father as supreme monarchs of this great earth, abounding in the seven treasures, you would still not have done enough to repay them. Why is that? Parents are very helpful to their children: they raise them, nurture them, and show them the world. But you have done enough, more than enough, to repay them if you encourage, settle, and ground unfaithful parents in faith, unethical parents in ethical conduct, stingy parents in generosity, or ignorant parents in wisdom.

items.plain: An untrue person is ungrateful and thankless, for that is all the wicked know how to be. A true person is grateful and thankful, for that is the nature of the good.
items.core_idea: Gratitude marks a good person

items.plain: An elder of eighty, ninety or a hundred who still burns for sensual pleasures counts as a child, not a senior. A young person in their prime who doesn't live for sensual pleasures counts as wise, a true senior.
items.core_idea: Maturity is freedom from craving, not age

items.plain: Train yourselves to have peaceful senses and a peaceful mind. Then what you do, say and think will be peaceful, and you can offer the gift of peace to your spiritual companions.
items.core_idea: A peaceful mind lets you give peace to others

items.plain: Good people live together this way: a senior mendicant thinks anyone, of any rank, should correct him and he should correct them. If corrected, he'd see it as kindness, say thank you, and fix what he did wrong.
items.core_idea: Welcome correction from anyone with thanks

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants there are two kinds of fools: one who carries the burden of what hasn't happened, and one who doesn't take up the burden of what has.
items.core_idea: Fools carry imagined burdens and drop real ones

items.plain: Defilements grow in two kinds of people: one who feels remorse over what they shouldn't, and one who feels no remorse over what they should.
items.core_idea: Misplaced remorse lets defilements grow

items.plain: Two hopes are hard to let go of: the hope for wealth and the hope for a long life.
items.core_idea: Hopes for wealth and long life are hard to drop

items.plain: Two kinds of people are rare in the world: one who takes the initiative to help, and one who is grateful and thankful.
items.core_idea: Initiative and gratitude are rare

items.plain: There are two things: cleansing your own mind, and not clinging to anything in the world.
items.core_idea: Cleanse your mind and cling to nothing

items.plain: A wise, capable good person keeps themselves healthy and whole, beyond reproach and full of merit, by two qualities: after careful examination, they criticize what deserves criticism and praise what deserves praise.
items.core_idea: Praise and criticize only after careful examination

items.plain: Fools and wise people alike are known by what they do, for wisdom shows itself in the traces it leaves.
items.core_idea: People are known by their deeds

items.plain: A wise person is known by three things: they recognize their own mistake, they deal with it properly, and they properly accept it when someone else confesses a mistake to them.
items.core_idea: Wisdom shows in how we handle mistakes

items.plain: A mendicant eats in moderation by reflecting that food is not for fun, indulgence or looks, but only to sustain the body, avoid harm and support spiritual practice, ending old discomfort without creating new, and living blamelessly and at ease.
items.core_idea: Eat to sustain the body, not for indulgence

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that bad conduct in body, speech and mind leads to hurting yourself, hurting others, and hurting both.
items.core_idea: Bad conduct hurts you and others

items.plain: A shopkeeper can gain more wealth or grow what they have by focusing carefully on their work in the morning, at midday and in the afternoon.
items.core_idea: Steady attention to work builds wealth

items.plain: There are three kinds of people: minds like an open sore, like lightning, and like diamond. The open-sore mind is irritable; even mild criticism makes them angry and bitter, like a festering sore that oozes more when struck.
items.core_idea: An irritable mind flares like a struck sore

items.plain: Spend time with people similar to you in ethics, meditation and wisdom. Because you share these, you can talk about them, the conversation flows, and you're both at ease.
items.core_idea: Keep company with those who share your values

items.plain: A person with speech like honey has given up harsh words; they speak gently, pleasantly and politely, in a way that reaches the heart and pleases people.
items.core_idea: Gentle speech that reaches the heart

items.plain: The Buddha says a family whose children honor their parents lives with divinity, with its first teachers, and with those worthy of offerings to the gods. These are all names for parents, who raise children and show them the world.
items.core_idea: Parents are divinity and first teachers

items.plain: Amid wealth and comfort, the Buddha reflected that ordinary people recoil at the old, forgetting they will age too. Since he would also grow old, recoiling made no sense, and he gave up the vanity of youth.
items.core_idea: We too will age, so drop the vanity of youth

items.plain: Sickness, old age and death are natural for everyone, yet ordinary people are disgusted by them in others. It would not be right for me to feel disgust, since my life is just the same.
items.core_idea: Sickness, age and death are shared by all

items.plain: There is no hiding place in the world for someone who does wrong. You yourself will know whether you lied or told the truth.
items.core_idea: You can't hide wrongdoing from yourself

items.plain: Life is very short and moves steadily on; for someone carried into old age there is no shelter. Seeing the danger in death, do good deeds that bring you joy.
items.core_idea: Life is short; do good while you can

items.plain: A person overcome by hate intends harm to themselves, others, or both, and suffers mental pain and sadness. Once hate is given up, they no longer intend harm and no longer suffer that pain.
items.core_idea: Hate harms everyone; giving it up ends the pain

items.plain: A deluded person doesn't truly know what is good for themselves, for others, or for both. Once delusion is given up, they truly understand it.
items.core_idea: Without delusion, we see what is truly good

items.plain: The noble truth of suffering: rebirth, old age, death, sorrow, pain and distress are suffering; so are meeting the disliked, losing the loved, and not getting what you want. In short, the five grasping aggregates are suffering.
items.core_idea: The noble truth: life as grasped is suffering

items.plain: Old age, sickness and death are three perils that tear mothers and children apart. Neither can take the other's place: a mother cannot age, sicken or die instead of her child, nor a child instead of their mother.
items.core_idea: No one can age, sicken or die for another

items.plain: The Buddha says he meditates by spreading a heart full of love in every direction, above, below and all around, to the whole world, abundant, boundless and free of hostility and ill will.
items.core_idea: Spread boundless love to the whole world

items.plain: The Buddha tells the Kālāmas not to accept things because of tradition, scripture, logic, a speaker's skill, or respect for a teacher. When you know for yourselves that something is unskillful and leads to harm and suffering, give it up.
items.core_idea: Test teachings by your own experience

items.plain: A noble disciple whose mind is free of ill will gains four comforts now: if there is an afterlife, a good rebirth; if not, a happy life; if wrongdoers suffer, no harm to them; if not, they know themselves pure.
items.core_idea: A pure heart is safe whatever the truth

items.plain: People who argue with hostility and arrogance hunt for each other's flaws and gloat when an opponent slips up and is beaten, but the noble ones don't discuss things like this.
items.core_idea: The noble don't argue to win

items.plain: Greed is mildly blameworthy but slow to fade. Hate is very blameworthy but quick to fade. Delusion is very blameworthy and slow to fade.
items.core_idea: Greed, hate and delusion differ in harm and persistence

items.plain: Perfected ones give up lying for life; they speak the truth, are honest and reliable, and don't deceive the world with words. For this day and night, I too will give up lying and be honest and dependable.
items.core_idea: Give up lying and speak the truth

items.plain: Greed destroys sight, vision and understanding. It blocks wisdom, sides with distress, and doesn't lead to extinguishment.
items.core_idea: Greed blinds and blocks wisdom

items.plain: If someone follows rules, a lifestyle and a spiritual path as the core of life, it bears fruit only if bad qualities decline and good ones grow; if the reverse happens, it bears no fruit.
items.core_idea: A practice is fruitful only if it makes you better

items.plain: The Buddha tells the mendicants that if you practice partly, you succeed partly; if you practice fully, you succeed fully. Either way, the training rules are not fruitless.
items.core_idea: Partial practice brings partial success

items.plain: The Buddha tells Kassapa he did make a mistake, but since he has recognized it and dealt with it properly, the Buddha accepts it. Growth in the training means recognizing a mistake, handling it properly and restraining yourself in future.
items.core_idea: Owning and correcting a mistake is growth
